entities.name: Erasmus Grasser
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Erasmus Grasser (d. 1518) was a pivotal Late Gothic sculptor and master builder whose prolific career profoundly shaped the artistic landscape of Munich and the wider Bavarian region at the cusp of the Renaissance. Active from the late 15th century until his death, Grasser's innovative approach to both wood sculpture and architectural design positioned him as a leading figure, transitioning from established medieval traditions towards the nascent humanism of the early modern period. His work is characterized by a dynamic expressiveness and a remarkable attention to detail, establishing a distinct Bavarian school of sculpture.

Grasser's most celebrated achievements include his series of ten 'Morris Dancers' (Moriskentänzer) carved between 1480 and 1481 for the festive hall of the Old Munich Town Hall, now housed in the Munich City Museum. These lively, characterful figures, depicting acrobatic and costumed dancers, exemplify his mastery in capturing movement and individual expression, moving beyond conventional religious iconography. As a master builder, he was instrumental in the construction and furnishing of significant ecclesiastical structures, including the Frauenkirche and St. Peter's Church in Munich, where his workshop produced numerous altarpieces, choir stalls, and architectural elements that defined the city's spiritual and civic spaces.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Erasmus Grasser was a leading master of Late Gothic sculpture and architecture in Bavaria, whose dynamic works, such as the 'Morris Dancers,' profoundly shaped the visual culture of Munich and influenced the transition towards early Renaissance styles in Southern Germany.
